title: Belonging Booster: Values Affirmation Exercise
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart describes a two-step classroom exercise in which students pick values they hold and write about why those values matter to them. He places it in the family of social-psychological wise interventions, small and precisely targeted acts that can have lasting effects. He cites Geoffrey Cohen's research, in which affirmed students, notably African American students, earned better grades for two or more years and the achievement gap narrowed. The mechanism is that affirming something important in a threatening context eases stereotype threat, and fear is what most undermines learning. He cautions that such interventions cannot simply be handed to students, since they depend on the teacher's skill and preparation. The post ends with a plug for his motivation course, but the practice and its rationale are well explained.
points: The exercise is simple: students choose a few personal values from a list and write why they matter, taking little class time.
Cohen's follow-up research found sustained grade gains and a narrowed achievement gap for students who received the intervention.
Stereotype threat shows that students can feel fear in classrooms despite the teacher's best efforts, and fear suppresses learning.
Affirming a deep value works better than telling students not to be afraid.
Like any non-silver-bullet, wise interventions need study, practice and thoughtful delivery.
quotes: The values affirmation intervention that I used is simple but well-informed. It’s what social psychologists call a “wise intervention,”* which Stanford researcher Geoffrey Cohen describe as “theoretically informed and precisely targeted,” that “even while small can have lasting effects.”**
1) Students look at a list of values and identify several values that they hold. 2) Students then write why these 2-3 values are important to them.

In the case of the values affirmation exercise, researchers followed students for two years afterwards, and they found that African American children who had received the intervention did better in their grades for the two (and in one case three) years that the study followed them. Importantly, these improvements led to a significant reduction in the achievement gap.

This phenomenon, which the research literature frequently labels “stereotype threat,” is a critical example of how fear so ruthlessly diminishes learning. And notice how these fears can exist in our classrooms despite even our best efforts!

And rather than telling students not to fear, which any parent knows is rarely effective, the values affirmation exercise allows students to affirm something of deep importance to them in a setting that may be threatening.

The thing with all of them is that they can’t be merely chucked at kids. Just like Doug Stark’s brilliantly spiraled Mechanics Instruction that Sticks series of warm-ups, results will vary based on the user’s skill and thoughtfulness.
Because they kill fear. They cultivate the key beliefs. They combat oppression.
